segments: ...the Caliph {OCR?} [witnessing] such things out of fear.
And there was a great tumult,
and about a hundred and fifty of the troops were killed,
and with difficulty they were pacified.
And in those days frequent earthquakes began to occur in Baghdad,
every day five or six times.
Now Sultan Sanjar sent an envoy to Sultan Mas'ud,
and with him two letters:
one secret,
in which he rebuked Mas'ud and mocked him,
saying, 'Why did you not kill the Caliph in the heat of battle?' And another, open letter, in which he said to him:
'At the very hour when you read these lines,
son (my son) Ghiyath al-Dunya wa'l-Din Mas'ud,
go in to the Commander of the Faithful,
and kiss the ground before him,
and seek pardon for your folly.
For I cannot bear the signs in heaven and on earth
which God is working on this account,
namely, winds, thunders, lightnings, and earthquakes of the earth.
And behold, the whole lower world is clothed in mourning,
and prayers have ceased,
and the doors of the mosques have been closed in all of Persia and Sinjar.
Henceforth, without any pretext or excuse, send him back with honor to his throne,
and deliver Dubays to him, so that he may do his will with him,
because he was the cause of all these evils.'
Then Mas'ud, when he understood these things,
gave orders, and they pitched large tents,
and he settled the Caliph in them.
And he carried the saddle-cloth before him for about half a parasang,
and brought him and lodged him in the great royal tent,
and sought pardon for his folly.
And he brought Dubays before him, bound in fetters,
and with him a sword and a burial shroud, and said:
'This man did everything,
and behold, I have delivered him into your hands;
command, and let it be done to him according as he has done.'
The Caliph, knowing that he was saying these things with his lips and not from the heart,
extended forgiveness even to Dubays.
Then Mas'ud began to urge the Caliph to go to Baghdad.
The Caliph, however, excused himself and said,
'I will not go
unless you go with me in person.'
And Mas'ud said,
'I will send emirs with you to be in your service,
and you may go in honor and sit in your residence.'
The Caliph, however, would not agree,
for he was afraid that they might set an ambush for him on the road,
and kill him by treachery,
because openly they did not [dare...]
